\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}

\title{Edge Effects Amplify Pollinator Decline in Fragmented Tropical Forests}
\author{C.~Mendoza, T.~Fitzgerald, and A.~Diallo}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Habitat fragmentation is a leading driver of biodiversity loss, yet its
indirect effects on species interactions remain poorly quantified. We
surveyed pollinator communities across 37 forest fragments in the
Atlantic Forest of Brazil, spanning three orders of magnitude in fragment
size, and measured visitation rates to a standardized array of flowering
plants. Pollinator abundance declined by 62\% and species richness by
45\% from forest interiors to edges, with the steepest declines occurring
within the first 100 m of forest edge. Small fragments ($<$10 ha) were
dominated by a single generalist bee species and exhibited visitation
rates comparable to open pasture. Structural equation models indicate
that edge effects on pollinators are mediated primarily through changes
in floral resource availability rather than microclimate. Our results
imply that conservation planning based on fragment area alone may
substantially underestimate functional pollinator loss, and that
buffer-zone management around fragment edges offers a cost-effective
mitigation strategy.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Tropical forests hold the majority of terrestrial species, yet they are
increasingly reduced to fragments embedded in agricultural matrices. When
a continuous forest is broken up, the resulting fragments experience
altered microclimates, increased hunting pressure, and shifts in species
composition along their edges. While the consequences of fragmentation
for plants and vertebrates are well documented, far less is known about
how fragmentation restructures the mutualistic interactions---such as
pollination---on which forest regeneration depends. Here we quantify how
pollinator communities and their visitation rates change from forest
interiors to edges across a fragmentation gradient in the Brazilian
Atlantic Forest.

\end{document}
